title: MENTOR: Learning from Failure with On-Policy Pedagogical Intervention

paper.title: MENTOR: Learning from Failure with On-Policy Pedagogical Intervention
paper.abstract: Abstract Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is a key driver for Large Reasoning Models, but it is vulnerable to "zero-reward collapse" , a training failure where a sudden increase in task difficulty causes the learning signal to vanish. We argue that the conventional approach of discarding these failed trajectories is wasteful, as they contain valuable diagnostic information about the model’s cognitive gaps, a bright side that can be leveraged for recovery. Existing solutions, however, often regress to static, "off-policy-style" interventions like pre-defined hint libraries or perform post-hoc refinement, failing to provide the adaptive, forward-looking guidance needed to escape the collapse. To address this, we propose a paradigm shift towards on-policy pedagogical intervention and introduce MENTOR , a multi-agent framework that acts as a live mentor. MENTOR diagnoses the root cause of failure in real-time and dynamically generates targeted, instructional prompts to guide the learning agent’s next attempt. As a plug-and-play module, MENTOR integrates seamlessly into existing policy optimization pipelines like GRPO without modifying the training infrastructure. Extensive experiments on math and code generation show that MENTOR effectively mitigates zero-reward collapse, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. Notably, it achieves massive average relative gains of up to 78.3% on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct over its base model.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large Reasoning Models have achieved remarkable progress in complex reasoning tasks such as mathematical problem solving and code generation ( Muennighoff et al., 2025 ; Min et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . These models generate detailed Chain-of-Thought reasoning traces, exhibit advanced behaviors including self-reflection and self-correction, and demonstrate generalization beyond their training distribution. A key driver of this progress is RLVR, which uses programmatic feedback to encourage exploration of diverse reasoning pathways and iterative strategy refinement. However, RLVR training is vulnerable to a critical failure mode. When task difficulty exceeds the model’s current capability boundary, all sampled reasoning trajectories can fail simultaneously. This results in zero reward for the entire batch, causing the learning signal to vanish and halting policy improvement. This phenomenon, which we term “zero-reward collapse”, arises from the misalignment between task complexity and model competence ( Gandhi et al., 2025 ; Team, 2024 ) . As illustrated in Figure 1 , once collapse occurs, the fraction of zero-reward samples rises rapidly and model performance plateaus immediately. Yet failed reasoning trajectories are not without value: each contains diagnostic information about where the error occurred, what cognitive deficiency it reflects, and what correction is needed. Discarding them entirely prevents the system from capturing real-time error patterns, leading to teaching signals misaligned with the true root causes of failure. This challenge exposes a fundamental tension in modern RL alignment. The field has progressed from off-policy methods like DPO ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) , which learn from static datasets, to on-policy methods like GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , which learn adaptively from real-time exploration. While on-policy learning is superior, its reliance on occasional success for gradient signals becomes its Achilles’ heel during zero-reward collapse. As compared in Figure 2 , existing solutions for this collapse fall short in several ways. Some resort to simply discarding the failed batches entirely (e.g., DAPO ( Yu et al., 2026 ) ), which wastes valuable diagnostic signals. Others regress to an “off-policy” style of intervention : they use static, pre-generated hint libraries (e.g., LUFFY ( Yan et al., 2026 ) , QUESTA ( Li et al., 2025b ) , HINT ( Wang et al., 2025 ) ) or pre-defined curricula (Scaf-GRPO ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) ). Even more advanced methods that perform post-hoc refinement of failed trajectories focus on output correction and data augmentation rather than providing the forward-looking guidance needed to escape the collapse (e.g., Critique-GRPO ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) , SRPO ( Wan et al., 2026 ) ). These static and reactive approaches cannot adapt to the model’s specific, evolving failure modes, creating a “distributional drift” where the guidance becomes misaligned and ineffective. We argue that the solution is not to abandon on-policy learning, but to augment it. What is needed is on-policy pedagogical intervention , a live mentor that diagnoses the root cause of failure in real-time and provides a targeted teaching signal to help the policy escape the collapse. To realize this vision, we propose MENTOR ( M ulti-agent E rror-aware N avigation and T eaching for O nline R einforcement learning), a framework that operationalizes on-policy pedagogical intervention. It enhances RLVR by converting moments of systemic failure into targeted teaching opportunities. An Attribution Agent identifies conceptual gaps and logical errors in failed trajectories; a Generation Agent creates targeted instructional prompts based on this diagnosis; a Judgment Agent validates prompt quality via formal rules and LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation; and a Repair Agent iteratively refines prompts using feedback. Together, they form a closed-loop teaching mechanism that integrates seamlessly into policy optimization pipelines such as GRPO without modifying the training infrastructure. Our main contributions are as follows: • We identify and formally characterize zero-reward collapse, a fundamental training bottleneck in RLVR. We argue that overcoming it requires a paradigm shift from static, off-policy-style fixes to dynamic, on-policy pedagogical intervention, exposing a shared structural limitation in existing RLVR methods. • We propose MENTOR, an end-to-end multi-agent framework for online pedagogical intervention in RLVR. To our knowledge, it is the first to embed feedback-driven, context-aware instructional prompting directly into the RLVR training loop. As a plug-and-play module, MENTOR constructs, validates, and iteratively refines targeted prompts without pre-built corpora, ensuring supervision remains aligned with the model’s current cognitive state throughout training. • We evaluate MENTOR on mathematical reasoning and code generation. Results show that MENTOR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving massive average relative gains of up to 78.3% on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct over its base model. MENTOR effectively mitigates training stagnation from zero-reward collapse and restores meaningful gradient signals .

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Figure 2: Comparison of mitigation strategies for zero-reward collapse in RLVR. The problem of zero-reward collapse has spurred various mitigation strategies. However, as illustrated in Figure 2 , existing approaches can be categorized by their underlying intervention philosophy, which, when analyzed, reveals a shared structural gap. They fall short of providing the on-policy pedagogical intervention necessary to resolve systemic training failure.

sections.heading: 2.1 Failure Avoidance via Filtering
sections.text: The most direct strategy is to simply sidestep the problem. Methods like DAPO ( Yu et al., 2026 ) employ hard-example filtering, identifying and discarding training batches where all rewards are zero. While this prevents the model from receiving degenerate gradient signals, it is a fundamentally passive approach. It treats systemic failure as an anomaly to be ignored rather than a symptom to be diagnosed. By filtering out the most challenging examples, this strategy offers no mechanism for the model to learn from its deepest cognitive errors and push its capability boundary.

sections.heading: 2.2 Static “Off-Policy” Guidance
sections.text: A more proactive set of methods attempts to provide external guidance, but does so using static, pre-generated resources, analogous to off-policy learning in RLHF. These approaches range from injecting high-quality reasoning traces from an offline corpus, as seen in LUFFY ( Yan et al., 2026 ) and QUESTA ( Li et al., 2025b ) , or pre-written conceptual heuristics as in HINT ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , to employing pre-defined curricula. For instance, Scaf-GRPO ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) uses a pre-built, hierarchical library of hints that are selected based on the model’s performance plateaus. While more structured than simple filtering, all these methods are fundamentally limited by their static nature. They rely on a fixed corpus of guidance that cannot adapt to the model’s specific, evolving failure modes during on-policy training. As the policy changes, its behavior inevitably diverges from the distribution of the offline data, leading to “distributional drift” . The pre-canned guidance becomes progressively less relevant, losing its effectiveness and potentially even destabilizing the learning process.

sections.heading: 2.3 Post-Hoc Refinement and Critique
sections.text: A more advanced paradigm focuses on learning from failure by refining or critiquing the model’s own outputs. This category includes a family of methods such as Critique-GRPO ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) , SRPO ( Wan et al., 2026 ) , CTRL ( Xie et al., 2025 ) , and Critique-RL ( Xi et al., 2025 ) . These frameworks analyze a failed trajectory and either generate a critique to refine it for data augmentation (Critique-GRPO) , train the policy to perform internal self-correction (SRPO) , or train a general-purpose critic model (CTRL, Critique-RL) . Although these methods are dynamic, their focus is retrospective and corrective, not prospective and pedagogical . They aim to “fix the answer” after the fact to create a better training sample. They do not, however, generate a targeted, forward-looking instructional hint designed to guide the model’s next reasoning attempt on the same problem. This is a critical distinction: they improve the data, but they do not directly teach the model the underlying cognitive skill it is missing, making them less effective at resolving systemic collapse.

sections.heading: 2.4 Distinctions from Foundational Methodologies
sections.text: Our work also builds upon and distinguishes itself from several foundational methodologies. For instance, the use of an LLM-as-a-Judge ( Gu et al., 2024 ) for automated evaluation and feedback-based prompt refinement at the inference stage ( Li et al., 2025a ) are powerful tools. However, MENTOR is the first to integrate this capability into a closed-loop, online RL training pipeline specifically to resolve training collapse. Similarly, our approach shares conceptual ground with knowledge distillation , where experience is transferred from a teacher to a student model ( Song and Zheng, 2026 ; Ma, 2023 ) . Yet, these methods typically rely on static, offline distillation and lack the ability to diagnose and fix inherent cognitive deficiencies in real-time ( Li et al., 2026 ; Jia et al., 2026 ) . In contrast, MENTOR’s framework can be seen as a highly dynamic, failure-driven form of distillation , generating teaching signals only when and where they are needed.

sections.heading: 2.5 The Unaddressed Gap: The Need for On-Policy Pedagogical Intervention
sections.text: Collectively, these strategies highlight a crucial, unaddressed gap in RLVR. Failure avoidance is too passive. Static guidance suffers from distributional drift. Post-hoc refinement is corrective, not pedagogical. None of these paradigms provide what is truly needed when an on-policy agent gets stuck: real-time, diagnostic intervention . No existing method performs a cognitive-level diagnosis of why the policy is systemically failing and then dynamically generates a targeted, instructional hint to guide its subsequent exploration. This is the core innovation of MENTOR. By establishing a closed-loop, multi-agent system for on-policy pedagogical intervention , MENTOR moves beyond avoidance, static guidance, and post-hoc refinement to actively teach the model how to overcome its current limitations, directly addressing the root cause of zero-reward collapse.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: Our method, MENTOR, is designed to overcome the "zero-reward collapse" problem in RLVR frameworks like GRPO. As illustrated in Figure 3 , MENTOR operates as a plug-and-play module that intercepts moments of systemic failure and transforms them into pedagogical opportunities. Instead of relying on static hint libraries, MENTOR generates instructional prompts on-demand, dynamically tailoring the teaching signal to the policy’s evolving cognitive gaps. The process consists of three main stages: (1) real-time detection of collapsed samples, (2) dynamic generation of pedagogical hints via a multi-agent system, and (3) seamless integration of these hints back into the training loop. Details of prompts are shown in Appendix A .

sections.heading: 3.1 Collapse-Aware Sample Filtering (CASF)
sections.text: The first stage is to identify instances of zero-reward collapse. This occurs when for a given problem instance q i q_{i} , all N N trajectories { τ j ( i ) } j = 1 N \{\tau_{j}^{(i)}\}_{j=1}^{N} sampled from the policy π θ \pi_{\theta} receive a reward of zero. Such a scenario leads to degenerate advantages and a vanishing gradient signal, halting learning for that instance. For example, consider the math problem q i q_{i} : "Determine whether there exists a nowhere dense set in ℝ \mathbb{R} that is not an F σ F_{\sigma} set." As detailed in Table 11 in Appendix B , the model might generate N = 4 N=4 trajectories, all incorrectly concluding "No" based on various flawed arguments. Since all trajectories fail verification, they all receive a reward of zero, triggering a collapse for this instance. To detect this, we introduce a lightweight hook into the training loop that executes after the reward scoring step. For each batch of training data, the hook identifies all instances where every sampled trajectory failed and collects them into a "collapse set" C C . If C C is empty, training proceeds normally. Otherwise, for each collapsed instance ( q i , a i ) ∈ C (q_{i},a_{i})\in C (where a i a_{i} is the ground-truth answer), we preserve the full set of failed trajectories { τ j ( i ) } j = 1 N \{\tau_{j}^{(i)}\}_{j=1}^{N} . These trajectories, while yielding no reward, contain valuable diagnostic information, revealing recurring error patterns that point to the model’s underlying misconceptions. The resulting triplet ( q i , a i , { τ j ( i ) } j = 1 N ) (q_{i},a_{i},\{\tau_{j}^{(i)}\}_{j=1}^{N}) for each collapsed instance is then passed to our guidance generation system.

sections.heading: 3.2 Failure-Driven Contextual Guidance (FDCG)
sections.text: To transform the diagnostic information from failed trajectories into a high-quality learning signal, we introduce a multi-agent system for FDCG. This system collaboratively synthesizes and validates targeted instructional hints. Continuing our example from Table 11 in Appendix B , the FDCG system receives the problem, the ground-truth answer ("Yes"), and the set of four failed trajectories. Formally, for each collapsed instance, the FDCG system, denoted by 𝒜 \mathcal{A} , generates a validated hint h i ∗ h_{i}^{*} by processing the failed trajectories in the context of the current policy π θ \pi_{\theta} : h i ∗ = 𝒜 ⁡ ( q i , a i , { τ j ( i ) } j = 1 N , π θ ) h_{i}^{*}=\mathcal{A}(q_{i},a_{i},\{\tau_{j}^{(i)}\}_{j=1}^{N};\pi_{\theta}) (1) This process is carried out by a sequence of specialized agents: Figure 3: Overview of the MENTOR framework. Attribution Agent. To provide targeted, rather than generic, guidance, we must first diagnose the specific cognitive error. The Attribution Agent is responsible for this diagnosis. Given the problem q i q_{i} , answer a i a_{i} , and the set of failed trajectories { τ j ( i ) } j = 1 N \{\tau_{j}^{(i)}\}_{j=1}^{N} , it analyzes the reasoning chains to identify persistent failure causes. In our example (Table 11 ), the agent analyzes the failed attempts and identifies that the model consistently misunderstands the relationship between topological properties, outputting a set of diagnostic keywords K i K_{i} : "Confused nowhere dense sets with F σ F_{\sigma} …". These keywords localize the conceptual gap without revealing the solution path. As the policy π θ \pi_{\theta} evolves, so do its failure modes, ensuring that the diagnosis from K i K_{i} remains tightly aligned with the model’s current deficiencies. Generation Agent. Based on the diagnosis, the Generation Agent acts as a pedagogical tutor. Using the diagnostic keywords K i K_{i} as a directive and the full set of failed trajectories as context, it generates a candidate instructional hint h ^ i \hat{h}_{i} . For instance, using the keywords from our example, the agent generates a candidate hint h ^ i \hat{h}_{i} : "Consider whether every nowhere dense …". It focuses on correcting the cognitive error while deliberately avoiding answer leakage or excessive reasoning steps, thereby encouraging the policy to rediscover the solution path itself. Judgment-Repair Loop. To ensure that generated hints are helpful, safe, and pedagogically sound, they undergo a rigorous closed-loop validation and refinement process. As shown in Table 11 in Appendix B , this initial hint undergoes a two-round refinement. In Round 1, the Judgment Agent evaluates the hint as "LOW" quality, critiquing it as "too vague". The Repair Agent uses this critique to generate a more directive version: "Hint: Think about whether a nowhere …". In Round 2, the Judgment Agent validates this refined hint as "HIGH" quality, making it the final output h i ∗ h_{i}^{*} . To prevent invalid teaching signals from entering the training pipeline, if a hint repeatedly fails validation, it is replaced by a pre-defined safe fallback hint. This two-tiered mechanism guarantees the pedagogical efficacy and safety of the final validated hint h i ∗ h_{i}^{*} .

sections.heading: 3.3 Integration into GRPO Training
sections.text: The final stage seamlessly injects the validated pedagogical guidance back into the GRPO training process to recover the learning signal. Hint Injection. For each collapsed sample ( q i , a i ) ∈ C (q_{i},a_{i})\in C , we form an augmented input by prepending the validated hint h i ∗ h_{i}^{*} to the original problem query: q i ′ = h i ∗ ⊕ q i q^{\prime}_{i}=h_{i}^{*}\oplus q_{i} , where ⊕ \oplus denotes concatenation. In our example, the new augmented input q i ′ q^{\prime}_{i} becomes: "Hint: Think about whether a nowhere… Original Question: Determine whether there…" Policy Update. This enhanced query q i ′ q^{\prime}_{i} replaces the original q i q_{i} and re-enters the standard GRPO training pipeline. With this targeted, pedagogical nudge, the policy π θ \pi_{\theta} is now significantly more likely to generate trajectories that receive non-zero rewards. As shown by the "New Rollout" section in Table 11 , the guided policy now generates several successful trajectories (e.g., New Rollouts 1, 2, and 4), correctly answering "Yes" by constructing a non-Borel subset of the Cantor set. These successful attempts receive non-zero rewards, restoring a meaningful gradient for this previously unsolvable problem. Crucially, MENTOR is training-objective-agnostic. It modifies only the input data for collapsed samples, leaving the GRPO loss function, optimizers, and reward mechanism entirely unchanged. sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Tasks and Models. We train MENTOR on complex reasoning in mathematical problem-solving (DeepMath-103K ( He et al., 2025 ) , 10K train/2.5K valid) and code generation (LiveCodeBench ( Jain et al., 2025 ) , 1,055 instances, 5:1 train/valid split). We test on a diverse set of models to assess cross-architecture transferability: math-specialized (Qwen2.5-Math-7B ( Yang et al., 2024 ) ), code-specialized (DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B ( Guo et al., 2024 ) ), lightweight (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B ( Guo et al., 2025 ) ), and general-purpose (Qwen3-4B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) ). For evaluation, we use a suite of standard benchmarks, including AIME ( Jia, 2024 ; Zhang and Team, 2025 ) , MATH-500 ( Lightman et al., 2024 ) , GAOKAO-Bench ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) and Olympiad-Bench ( He et al., 2024 ) for math, and HumanEval ( Chen et al., 2021 ) (HE), MBPP ( Austin et al., 2021 ) , and BigCodeBench ( Zhuo et al., 2025 ) (BCB) for code. We also test out-of-distribution generalization on MMLU ( Hendrycks et al., 2020 ) . Training Details. All experiments are conducted on eight H20-3E GPUs. We train for one epoch with a learning rate of 1 × 10 − 6 1\times 10^{-6} and sample four trajectories per problem. The pedagogical agents within MENTOR (e.g., for hint generation and critique) are powered by Qwen3-32B. Baselines. We compare MENTOR against eight State-of-the-Art(SOTA) baselines representing the primary paradigms for mitigating zero-reward collapse. These include the standard on-policy algorithm with no mitigation , (1) Vanilla GRPO(GRPO) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) ; a failure avoidance method, (2) DAPO ( Yu et al., 2026 ) , which filters out zero-reward batches; post-hoc refinement methods such as (3) Critique-GRPO(Critique) ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) and (4) SRPO ( Wan et al., 2026 ) , which critique or refine failed trajectories for data augmentation; and finally, methods using static, off-policy guidance from pre-defined hint libraries or curricula, including (5) LUFFY ( Yan et al., 2026 ) , (6) QUESTA ( Li et al., 2025b ) , (7) HINT ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , and (8) Scaf-GRPO ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) . The hints required by all baselines are generated by the same Qwen3-32B model under a matched generation budget .

sections.heading: 4.2 Main Results
sections.text: As shown in Tables 1 and 2 , MENTOR consistently outperforms all baseline strategies across both mathematical reasoning and code generation tasks, validating the superiority of on-policy pedagogical intervention. Compared to Vanilla GRPO, which often stagnates due to zero-reward collapse, MENTOR achieves massive average relative gains, such as +19.8% on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B for math and +20.8% for code . This demonstrates that actively converting failures into teaching moments is far more effective than simply waiting for sporadic successes. MENTOR also surpasses passive failure avoidance strategies like DAPO, confirming our core hypothesis that discarding failed trajectories is wasteful, and leveraging their diagnostic information for targeted intervention is critical for recovery . Furthermore, MENTOR consistently outperforms methods using static, off-policy guidance like QUESTA, HINT, and Scaf-GRPO. For instance, on the math-specialized Qwen2.5-Math-7B, MENTOR achieves a 50.0% relative gain, surpassing all static baselines. This confirms that dynamic, on-policy adaptation to the model’s evolving failure modes is superior to static guidance that suffers from distributional drift . Similarly, MENTOR proves more effective than post-hoc refinement methods like Critique-GRPO. Its forward-looking, pedagogical guidance teaches the model the underlying skill it is missing, proving more effective at resolving systemic collapse than the retrospective, corrective feedback of refinement-based approaches. MENTOR’s impact is particularly pronounced on smaller or less-specialized models, which are more susceptible to zero-reward collapse. On the lightweight DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, MENTOR boosts math accuracy by 35.2% and code accuracy by 43.6% relative to the base model. On the general-purpose Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, it achieves a remarkable 78.3% relative gain in math. These results show that MENTOR’s targeted instructional signals effectively overcome training stagnation and unlock the latent reasoning potential of these models . Even on highly specialized models like DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B, MENTOR delivers a 24.7% relative gain, showing that its failure-attribution-driven teaching is beneficial even for tuned models. To assess whether MENTOR learns robust reasoning rather than in-domain pattern matching, we evaluate out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization on MMLU. As shown in Table 1 , MENTOR consistently outperforms or matches the best baselines on MMLU across all four models (e.g., achieving a 66.7% relative gain on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B). This strong transfer to unseen, knowledge-intensive tasks indicates that MENTOR helps the model capture deeper, generalizable reasoning structures rather than superficial correlations, significantly enhancing model robustness .

sections.heading: 4.3 Efficiency and Cost-Benefit Analysis
sections.text: MENTOR offers a practical and scalable solution by automating the pedagogical process. As illustrated in Table 3 , unlike strong hint-based baselines such as Scaf-GRPO and QUESTA, which rely on costly and labor-intensive offline data preparation (about 24 expert hours), MENTOR eliminates this manual effort entirely. The reported costs include Qwen3-32B multi-agent inference. Moreover, compared to other online methods like Critique-GRPO that suffer from computational bottlenecks, MENTOR is approximately 24% faster in wall-clock time (17.9h vs. 23.5h) . While the FDCG module introduces a marginal computational overhead compared to vanilla GRPO (a modest 2.6 hours on Qwen3-4B), this small investment represents a highly effective trade-off. This is because it (1) Delivers significant performance improvements , achieving average relative gains of up to +78.3% (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct on math), and (2) Enables dynamic adaptivity by producing high-quality, targeted hints to prevent reward collapse and adapt to the model’s evolving failure modes, a crucial capability that vanilla GRPO lacks entirely. sections.heading: 4.4.2 Hyperparameter Analysis.
sections.text: We analyze two key hyperparameters, Max Retry (number of full hint generation attempts) and Max Refine (internal refinement iterations), as shown in Figure 4 . Max Retry. Across both math and code, performance consistently peaks at Max Retry = 2. A value of 1 lacks fault tolerance against poor initial hints, while a value of 3 introduces redundant or noisy prompts. This shows that a balanced number of attempts is crucial for generating diverse yet high-quality guidance . Max Refine. The optimal Max Refine value varies by model and task, reflecting differences in error complexity. For instance, Qwen3-4B peaks at Max Refine = 2 for math, while the smaller Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct benefits from more refinement (Max Refine = 3). This indicates that more complex or subtle error patterns require deeper semantic analysis and restructuring within the Judgment-Repair loop . sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We propose MENTOR to address the training bottleneck in RLVR caused by zero-reward collapse. It dynamically identifies policy failures during online learning, attributes underlying cognitive errors, and guides the agent with structured teaching prompts for targeted policy refinement, thereby surpassing the learning limits of existing approaches. Experiments show that MENTOR achieves strong generalization across model scales and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on challenging benchmarks in mathematical reasoning and code generation. By actively focusing on hard examples and enabling learning from failure, MENTOR not only enhances complex task performance but also overcomes the training ceiling imposed by zero-reward collapse.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: The current prompt generation and reasoning guidance mechanism is only validated in single-modal scenarios, while its applicability in complex dynamic environments and multi-modal fusion tasks has not been fully explored.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.13594v1 [cs.AI] 09 Oct 2026 MENTOR: Learning from Failure with On-Policy Pedagogical Intervention Guanlan Yue Hang Yu Xiaoyong Huang Ruipeng Li Affiliation: Wei Zhang , Bingchang Liu , Rui Wang Affiliation: Correspondence: gl2002@stu.xjtu.edu.cn Abstract Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is a key driver for Large Reasoning Models, but it is vulnerable to "zero-reward collapse" , a training failure where a sudden increase in task difficulty causes the learning signal to vanish. We argue that the conventional approach of discarding these failed trajectories is wasteful, as they contain valuable diagnostic information about the model’s cognitive gaps, a bright side that can be leveraged for recovery. Existing solutions, however, often regress to static, "off-policy-style" interventions like pre-defined hint libraries or perform post-hoc refinement, failing to provide the adaptive, forward-looking guidance needed to escape the collapse. To address this, we propose a paradigm shift towards on-policy pedagogical intervention and introduce MENTOR , a multi-agent framework that acts as a live mentor. MENTOR diagnoses the root cause of failure in real-time and dynamically generates targeted, instructional prompts to guide the learning agent’s next attempt. As a plug-and-play module, MENTOR integrates seamlessly into existing policy optimization pipelines like GRPO without modifying the training infrastructure. Extensive experiments on math and code generation show that MENTOR effectively mitigates zero-reward collapse, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. Notably, it achieves massive average relative gains of up to 78.3% on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct over its base model. Figure 1: Deepseek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B ( Guo et al., 2025 ) math reasoning training dynamics. 1 Introduction Large Reasoning Models have achieved remarkable progress in complex reasoning tasks such as mathematical problem solving and code generation ( Muennighoff et al., 2025 ; Min et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . These models generate detailed Chain-of-Thought reasoning traces, exhibit advanced behaviors including self-reflection and self-correction, and demonstrate generalization beyond their training distribution. A key driver of this progress is RLVR, which uses programmatic feedback to encourage exploration of diverse reasoning pathways and iterative strategy refinement. However, RLVR training is vulnerable to a critical failure mode. When task difficulty exceeds the model’s current capability boundary, all sampled reasoning trajectories can fail simultaneously. This results in zero reward for the entire batch, causing the learning signal to vanish and halting policy improvement. This phenomenon, which we term “zero-reward collapse”, arises from the misalignment between task complexity and model competence ( Gandhi et al., 2025 ; Team, 2024 ) . As illustrated in Figure 1 , once collapse occurs, the fraction of zero-reward samples rises rapidly and model performance plateaus immediately. Yet failed reasoning trajectories are not without value: each contains diagnostic information about where the error occurred, what cognitive deficiency it reflects, and what correction is needed. Discarding them entirely prevents the system from capturing real-time error patterns, leading to teaching signals misaligned with the true root causes of failure. This challenge exposes a fundamental tension in modern RL alignment. The field has progressed from off-policy methods like DPO ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) , which learn from static datasets, to on-policy methods like GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , which learn adaptively from real-time exploration. While on-policy learning is superior, its reliance on occasional success for gradient signals becomes its Achilles’ heel during zero-reward collapse. As compared in Figure 2 , existing solutions for this collapse fall short in several ways. Some resort to simply discarding the failed batches entirely (e.g., DAPO ( Yu et al., 2026 ) ), which wastes valuable diagnostic signals. Others regress to an “off-policy” style of intervention : they use static, pre-generated hint libraries (e.g., LUFFY ( Yan et al., 2026 ) , QUESTA ( Li et al., 2025b ) , HINT ( Wang et al., 2025 ) ) or pre-defined curricula (Scaf-GRPO ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) ). Even more advanced methods that perform post-hoc refinement of failed trajectories focus on output correction and data augmentation rather than providing the forward-looking guidance needed to escape the collapse (e.g., Critique-GRPO ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) , SRPO ( Wan et al., 2026 ) ). These static and reactive approaches cannot adapt to the model’s specific, evolving failure modes, creating a “distributional drift” where the guidance becomes misaligned and ineffective. We argue that the solution is not to abandon on-policy learning, but to augment it. What is needed is on-policy pedagogical intervention , a live mentor that diagnoses the root cause of failure in real-time and provides a targeted teaching signal to help the policy escape the collapse. To realize this vision, we propose MENTOR ( M ulti-agent E rror-aware N avigation and T eaching for O nline R einforcement learning), a framework that operationalizes on-policy pedagogical intervention. It enhances RLVR by converting moments of systemic failure into targeted teaching opportunities. An Attribution Agent identifies conceptual gaps and logical errors in failed trajectories; a Generation Agent creates targeted instructional prompts based on this diagnosis; a Judgment Agent validates prompt quality via formal rules and LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation; and a Repair Agent iteratively refines prompts using feedback. Together, they form a closed-loop teaching mechanism that integrates seamlessly into policy optimization pipelines such as GRPO without modifying the training infrastructure. Our main contributions are as follows: • We identify and formally characterize zero-reward collapse, a fundamental training bottleneck in RLVR. We argue that overcoming it requires a paradigm shift from static, off-policy-style fixes to dynamic, on-policy pedagogical intervention, exposing a shared structural limitation in existing RLVR methods. • We propose MENTOR, an end-to-end multi-agent framework for online pedagogical intervention in RLVR. To our knowledge, it is the first to embed feedback-driven, context-aware instructional prompting directly into the RLVR training loop. As a plug-and-play module, MENTOR constructs, validates, and iteratively refines targeted prompts without pre-built corpora, ensuring supervision remains aligned with the model’s current cognitive state throughout training. • We evaluate MENTOR on mathematical reasoning and code generation. Results show that MENTOR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving massive average relative gains of up to 78.3% on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct over its base model. MENTOR effectively mitigates training stagnation from zero-reward collapse and restores meaningful gradient signals . 2 Related Work Figure 2: Comparison of mitigation strategies for zero-reward collapse in RLVR. The problem of zero-reward collapse has spurred various mitigation strategies. However, as illustrated in Figure 2 , existing approaches can be categorized by their underlying intervention philosophy, which, when analyzed, reveals a shared structural gap. They fall short of providing the on-policy pedagogical intervention necessary to resolve systemic training failure. 2.1 Failure Avoidance via Filtering The most direct strategy is to simply sidestep the problem. Methods like DAPO ( Yu et al., 2026 ) employ hard-example filtering, identifying and discarding training batches where all rewards are zero. While this prevents the model from receiving degenerate gradient signals, it is a fundamentally passive approach. It treats systemic failure as an anomaly to be ignored rather than a symptom to be diagnosed. By filtering out the most challenging examples, this strategy offers no mechanism for the model to learn from its deepest cognitive errors and push its capability boundary. 2.2 Static “Off-Policy” Guidance A more proactive set of methods attempts to provide external guidance, but does so using static, pre-generated resources, analogous to off-policy learning in RLHF. These approaches range from injecting high-quality reasoning traces from an offline corpus, as seen in LUFFY ( Yan et al., 2026 ) and QUESTA ( Li et al., 2025b ) , or pre-written conceptual heuristics as in HINT ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , to employing pre-defined curricula. For instance, Scaf-GRPO ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) uses a pre-built, hierarchical library of hints that are selected based on the model’s performance plateaus. While more structured than simple filtering, all these methods are fundamentally limited by their static nature. They rely on a fixed corpus of guidance that cannot adapt to the model’s specific, evolving failure modes during on-policy training. As the policy changes, its behavior inevitably diverges from the distribution of the offline data, leading to “distributional drift” . The pre-canned guidance becomes progressively less relevant, losing its effectiveness and potentially even destabilizing the learning process. 2.3 Post-Hoc Refinement and Critique A more advanced paradigm focuses on learning from failure by refining or critiquing the model’s own outputs. This category includes a family of methods such as Critique-GRPO ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) , SRPO ( Wan et al., 2026 ) , CTRL ( Xie et al., 2025 ) , and Critique-RL ( Xi et al., 2025 ) . These frameworks analyze a failed trajectory and either generate a critique to refine it for data augmentation (Critique-GRPO) , train the policy to perform internal self-correction (SRPO) , or train a general-purpose critic model (CTRL, Critique-RL) . Although these methods are dynamic, their focus is retrospective and corrective, not prospective and pedagogical . They aim to “fix the answer” after the fact to create a better training sample. They do not, however, generate a targeted, forward-looking instructional hint designed to guide the model’s next reasoning attempt on the same problem. This is a critical distinction: they improve the data, but they do not directly teach the model the underlying cognitive skill it is missing, making them less effective at resolving systemic collapse. 2.4 Distinctions from Foundational Methodologies Our work also builds upon and distinguishes itself from several foundational methodologies. For instance, the use of an LLM-as-a-Judge ( Gu et al., 2024 ) for automated evaluation and feedback-based prompt refinement at the inference stage ( Li et al., 2025a ) are powerful tools. However, MENTOR is the first to integrate this capability into a closed-loop, online RL training pipeline specifically to resolve training collapse. Similarly, our approach shares conceptual ground with knowledge distillation , where experience is transferred from a teacher to a student model ( Song and Zheng, 2026 ; Ma, 2023 ) . Yet, these methods typically rely on static, offline distillation and lack the ability to diagnose and fix inherent cognitive deficiencies in real-time ( Li et al., 2026 ; Jia et al., 2026 ) . In contrast, MENTOR’s framework can be seen as a highly dynamic, failure-driven form of distillation , generating teaching signals only when and where they are needed. 2.5 The Unaddressed Gap: The Need for On-Policy Pedagogical Intervention Collectively, these strategies highlight a crucial, unaddressed gap in RLVR. Failure avoidance is too passive. Static guidance suffers from distributional drift. Post-hoc refinement is corrective, not pedagogical. None of these paradigms provide what is truly needed when an on-policy agent gets stuck: real-time, diagnostic intervention . No existing method performs a cognitive-level diagnosis of why the policy is systemically failing and then dynamically generates a targeted, instructional hint to guide its subsequent exploration. This is the core innovation of MENTOR. By establishing a closed-loop, multi-agent system for on-policy pedagogical intervention , MENTOR moves beyond avoidance, static guidance, and post-hoc refinement to actively teach the model how to overcome its current limitations, directly addressing the root cause of zero-reward collapse. 3 Method Our method, MENTOR, is designed to overcome the "zero-reward collapse" problem in RLVR frameworks like GRPO. As illustrated in Figure 3 , MENTOR operates as a plug-and-play module that intercepts moments of systemic failure and transforms them into pedagogical opportunities. Instead of relying on static hint libraries, MENTOR generates instructional prompts on-demand, dynamically tailoring the teaching signal to the policy’s evolving cognitive gaps. The process consists of three main stages: (1) real-time detection of collapsed samples, (2) dynamic generation of pedagogical hints via a multi-agent system, and (3) seamless integration of these hints back into the training loop. Details of prompts are shown in Appendix A . 3.1 Collapse-Aware Sample Filtering (CASF) The first stage is to identify instances of zero-reward collapse. This occurs when for a given problem instance q i q_{i} , all N N trajectories { τ j ( i ) } j = 1 N \{\tau_{j}^{(i)}\}_{j=1}^{N} sampled from the policy π θ \pi_{\theta} receive a reward of zero. Such a scenario leads to degenerate advantages and a vanishing gradient signal, halting learning for that instance. For example, consider the math problem q i q_{i} : "Determine whether there exists a nowhere dense set in ℝ \mathbb{R} that is not an F σ F_{\sigma} set." As detailed in Table 11 in Appendix B , the model might generate N = 4 N=4 trajectories, all incorrectly concluding "No" based on various flawed arguments. Since all trajectories fail verification, they all receive a reward of zero, triggering a collapse for this instance. To detect this, we introduce a lightweight hook into the training loop that executes after the reward scoring step. For each batch of training data, the hook identifies all instances where every sampled trajectory failed and collects them into a "collapse set" C C . If C C is empty, training proceeds normally. Otherwise, for each collapsed instance ( q i , a i ) ∈ C (q_{i},a_{i})\in C (where a i a_{i} is the ground-truth answer), we preserve the full set of failed trajectories { τ j ( i ) } j = 1 N \{\tau_{j}^{(i)}\}_{j=1}^{N} . These trajectories, while yielding no reward, contain valuable diagnostic information, revealing recurring error patterns that point to the model’s underlying misconceptions. The resulting triplet ( q i , a i , { τ j ( i ) } j = 1 N ) (q_{i},a_{i},\{\tau_{j}^{(i)}\}_{j=1}^{N}) for each collapsed instance is then passed to our guidance generation system. 3.2 Failure-Driven Contextual Guidance (FDCG) To transform the diagnostic information from failed trajectories into a high-quality learning signal, we introduce a multi-agent system for FDCG. This system collaboratively synthesizes and validates targeted instructional hints. Continuing our example from Table 11 in Appendix B , the FDCG system receives the problem, the ground-truth answer ("Yes"), and the set of four failed trajectories. Formally, for each collapsed instance, the FDCG system, denoted by 𝒜 \mathcal{A} , generates a validated hint h i ∗ h_{i}^{*} by processing the failed trajectories in the context of the current policy π θ \pi_{\theta} : h i ∗ = 𝒜 ⁡ ( q i , a i , { τ j ( i ) } j = 1 N , π θ ) h_{i}^{*}=\mathcal{A}(q_{i},a_{i},\{\tau_{j}^{(i)}\}_{j=1}^{N};\pi_{\theta}) (1) This process is carried out by a sequence of specialized agents: Figure 3: Overview of the MENTOR framework. Attribution Agent. To provide targeted, rather than generic, guidance, we must first diagnose the specific cognitive error. The Attribution Agent is responsible for this diagnosis. Given the problem q i q_{i} , answer a i a_{i} , and the set of failed trajectories { τ j ( i ) } j = 1 N \{\tau_{j}^{(i)}\}_{j=1}^{N} , it analyzes the reasoning chains to identify persistent failure causes. In our example (Table 11 ), the agent analyzes the failed attempts and identifies that the model consistently misunderstands the relationship between topological properties, outputting a set of diagnostic keywords K i K_{i} : "Confused nowhere dense sets with F σ F_{\sigma} …". These keywords localize the conceptual gap without revealing the solution path. As the policy π θ \pi_{\theta} evolves, so do its failure modes, ensuring that the diagnosis from K i K_{i} remains tightly aligned with the model’s current deficiencies. Generation Agent. Based on the diagnosis, the Generation Agent acts as a pedagogical tutor. Using the diagnostic keywords K i K_{i} as a directive and the full set of failed trajectories as context, it generates a candidate instructional hint h ^ i \hat{h}_{i} . For instance, using the keywords from our example, the agent generates a candidate hint h ^ i \hat{h}_{i} : "Consider whether every nowhere dense …". It focuses on correcting the cognitive error while deliberately avoiding answer leakage or excessive reasoning steps, thereby encouraging the policy to rediscover the solution path itself. Judgment-Repair Loop. To ensure that generated hints are helpful, safe, and pedagogically sound, they undergo a rigorous closed-loop validation and refinement process. As shown in Table 11 in Appendix B , this initial hint undergoes a two-round refinement. In Round 1, the Judgment Agent evaluates the hint as "LOW" quality, critiquing it as "too vague". The Repair Agent uses this critique to generate a more directive version: "Hint: Think about whether a nowhere …". In Round 2, the Judgment Agent validates this refined hint as "HIGH" quality, making it the final output h i ∗ h_{i}^{*} . To prevent invalid teaching signals from entering the training pipeline, if a hint repeatedly fails validation, it is replaced by a pre-defined safe fallback hint. This two-tiered mechanism guarantees the pedagogical efficacy and safety of the final validated hint h i ∗ h_{i}^{*} . 3.3 Integration into GRPO Training The final stage seamlessly injects the validated pedagogical guidance back into the GRPO training process to recover the learning signal. Hint Injection. For each collapsed sample ( q i , a i ) ∈ C (q_{i},a_{i})\in C , we form an augmented input by prepending the validated hint h i ∗ h_{i}^{*} to the original problem query: q i ′ = h i ∗ ⊕ q i q^{\prime}_{i}=h_{i}^{*}\oplus q_{i} , where ⊕ \oplus denotes concatenation. In our example, the new augmented input q i ′ q^{\prime}_{i} becomes: "Hint: Think about whether a nowhere… Original Question: Determine whether there…" Policy Update. This enhanced query q i ′ q^{\prime}_{i} replaces the original q i q_{i} and re-enters the standard GRPO training pipeline. With this targeted, pedagogical nudge, the policy π θ \pi_{\theta} is now significantly more likely to generate trajectories that receive non-zero rewards. As shown by the "New Rollout" section in Table 11 , the guided policy now generates several successful trajectories (e.g., New Rollouts 1, 2, and 4), correctly answering "Yes" by constructing a non-Borel subset of the Cantor set. These successful attempts receive non-zero rewards, restoring a meaningful gradient for this previously unsolvable problem. Crucially, MENTOR is training-objective-agnostic. It modifies only the input data for collapsed samples, leaving the GRPO loss function, optimizers, and reward mechanism entirely unchanged. We train MENTOR on complex reasoning in mathematical problem-solving (DeepMath-103K ( He et al., 2025 ) , 10K train/2.5K valid) and code generation (LiveCodeBench ( Jain et al., 2025 ) , 1,055 instances, 5:1 train/valid split). We test on a diverse set of models to assess cross-architecture transferability: math-specialized (Qwen2.5-Math-7B ( Yang et al., 2024 ) ), code-specialized (DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B ( Guo et al., 2024 ) ), lightweight (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B ( Guo et al., 2025 ) ), and general-purpose (Qwen3-4B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) ). For evaluation, we use a suite of standard benchmarks, including AIME ( Jia, 2024 ; Zhang and Team, 2025 ) , MATH-500 ( Lightman et al., 2024 ) , GAOKAO-Bench ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) and Olympiad-Bench ( He et al., 2024 ) for math, and HumanEval ( Chen et al., 2021 ) (HE), MBPP ( Austin et al., 2021 ) , and BigCodeBench ( Zhuo et al., 2025 ) (BCB) for code. We also test out-of-distribution generalization on MMLU ( Hendrycks et al., 2020 ) . Training Details. All experiments are conducted on eight H20-3E GPUs. We train for one epoch with a learning rate of 1 × 10 − 6 1\times 10^{-6} and sample four trajectories per problem. The pedagogical agents within MENTOR (e.g., for hint generation and critique) are powered by Qwen3-32B. Baselines. We compare MENTOR against eight State-of-the-Art(SOTA) baselines representing the primary paradigms for mitigating zero-reward collapse. These include the standard on-policy algorithm with no mitigation , (1) Vanilla GRPO(GRPO) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) ; a failure avoidance method, (2) DAPO ( Yu et al., 2026 ) , which filters out zero-reward batches; post-hoc refinement methods such as (3) Critique-GRPO(Critique) ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) and (4) SRPO ( Wan et al., 2026 ) , which critique or refine failed trajectories for data augmentation; and finally, methods using static, off-policy guidance from pre-defined hint libraries or curricula, including (5) LUFFY ( Yan et al., 2026 ) , (6) QUESTA ( Li et al., 2025b ) , (7) HINT ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , and (8) Scaf-GRPO ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) . The hints required by all baselines are generated by the same Qwen3-32B model under a matched generation budget . 4.2 Main Results As shown in Tables 1 and 2 , MENTOR consistently outperforms all baseline strategies across both mathematical reasoning and code generation tasks, validating the superiority of on-policy pedagogical intervention. Compared to Vanilla GRPO, which often stagnates due to zero-reward collapse, MENTOR achieves massive average relative gains, such as +19.8% on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B for math and +20.8% for code . This demonstrates that actively converting failures into teaching moments is far more effective than simply waiting for sporadic successes. MENTOR also surpasses passive failure avoidance strategies like DAPO, confirming our core hypothesis that discarding failed trajectories is wasteful, and leveraging their diagnostic information for targeted intervention is critical for recovery . Furthermore, MENTOR consistently outperforms methods using static, off-policy guidance like QUESTA, HINT, and Scaf-GRPO. For instance, on the math-specialized Qwen2.5-Math-7B, MENTOR achieves a 50.0% relative gain, surpassing all static baselines. This confirms that dynamic, on-policy adaptation to the model’s evolving failure modes is superior to static guidance that suffers from distributional drift . Similarly, MENTOR proves more effective than post-hoc refinement methods like Critique-GRPO. Its forward-looking, pedagogical guidance teaches the model the underlying skill it is missing, proving more effective at resolving systemic collapse than the retrospective, corrective feedback of refinement-based approaches. MENTOR’s impact is particularly pronounced on smaller or less-specialized models, which are more susceptible to zero-reward collapse. On the lightweight DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, MENTOR boosts math accuracy by 35.2% and code accuracy by 43.6% relative to the base model. On the general-purpose Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, it achieves a remarkable 78.3% relative gain in math. These results show that MENTOR’s targeted instructional signals effectively overcome training stagnation and unlock the latent reasoning potential of these models . Even on highly specialized models like DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B, MENTOR delivers a 24.7% relative gain, showing that its failure-attribution-driven teaching is beneficial even for tuned models. To assess whether MENTOR learns robust reasoning rather than in-domain pattern matching, we evaluate out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization on MMLU. As shown in Table 1 , MENTOR consistently outperforms or matches the best baselines on MMLU across all four models (e.g., achieving a 66.7% relative gain on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B). This strong transfer to unseen, knowledge-intensive tasks indicates that MENTOR helps the model capture deeper, generalizable reasoning structures rather than superficial correlations, significantly enhancing model robustness . 4.3 Efficiency and Cost-Benefit Analysis MENTOR offers a practical and scalable solution by automating the pedagogical process. As illustrated in Table 3 , unlike strong hint-based baselines such as Scaf-GRPO and QUESTA, which rely on costly and labor-intensive offline data preparation (about 24 expert hours), MENTOR eliminates this manual effort entirely. The reported costs include Qwen3-32B multi-agent inference. Moreover, compared to other online methods like Critique-GRPO that suffer from computational bottlenecks, MENTOR is approximately 24% faster in wall-clock time (17.9h vs. 23.5h) . While the FDCG module introduces a marginal computational overhead compared to vanilla GRPO (a modest 2.6 hours on Qwen3-4B), this small investment represents a highly effective trade-off. This is because it (1) Delivers significant performance improvements , achieving average relative gains of up to +78.3% (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct on math), and (2) Enables dynamic adaptivity by producing high-quality, targeted hints to prevent reward collapse and adapt to the model’s evolving failure modes, a crucial capability that vanilla GRPO lacks entirely. It dynamically identifies policy failures during online learning, attributes underlying cognitive errors, and guides the agent with structured teaching prompts for targeted policy refinement, thereby surpassing the learning limits of existing approaches. Experiments show that MENTOR achieves strong generalization across model scales and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on challenging benchmarks in mathematical reasoning and code generation. By actively focusing on hard examples and enabling learning from failure, MENTOR not only enhances complex task performance but also overcomes the training ceiling imposed by zero-reward collapse. Limitations The current prompt generation and reasoning guidance mechanism is only validated in single-modal scenarios, while its applicability in complex dynamic environments and multi-modal fusion tasks has not been fully explored.
